application.name: ofetch
application.summary: A TypeScript HTTP client library that wraps the Fetch API with automatic request handling, response parsing, retries, timeouts, error normalization, and lifecycle hooks.
application.purpose: Provides a developer-friendly fetch interface for making HTTP requests in browser, edge, and Node.js environments while reducing repetitive request setup and error-handling code.

domains.name: HTTP Client
domains.description: Primary domain. Handles outbound HTTP requests, request configuration, URL and header construction, payload serialization, response parsing, and response-type selection.

domains.name: Request Resilience
domains.description: Adds retry handling for transient failures, configurable retry delays, status-code policies, and timeout-based request cancellation.

domains.name: Error Handling
domains.description: Normalizes HTTP and transport failures into a FetchError containing request, response, and parsed error data.

domains.name: Lifecycle Observability
domains.description: Provides hooks around request, response, and error phases for custom middleware, logging, tracing, and instrumentation.

domains.name: Cross-Runtime Compatibility
domains.description: Supports global Fetch API implementations while providing Node.js-specific transport and optional keep-alive behavior.

entityAnnotations.businessMeaning: Core request orchestrator. Creates the enhanced fetch client, resolves defaults, applies URL and header rules, prepares payloads, invokes lifecycle hooks, parses responses, and delegates failures to retry or error-normalization logic.
Central failure policy. Decides whether a failed request should be retried, applies retry delays and status eligibility, and otherwise converts the failure into a normalized client error.
Builds a normalized error from request context, preserving the HTTP method, URL, response status, response data, and underlying cause for diagnosis.
Produces the effective request configuration by combining global defaults with per-call options and merging headers and query parameters.
Combines default and request-specific headers, with request-specific values taking precedence.
Identifies HTTP methods that are treated as carrying request payloads, such as POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.
Determines whether a request body can be automatically serialized as JSON, excluding values such as streams, form data, and binary buffers.
Chooses an appropriate response representation from the response content type, with special handling for JSON, server-sent events, text, and binary content.
Executes lifecycle callbacks in order, awaiting asynchronous callbacks so instrumentation or middleware can complete before the request proceeds.
Creates the Node.js transport used by the client. It uses the platform's global fetch when available and otherwise falls back to a compatible implementation with optional HTTP keep-alive agents.
Demonstrates that callers can specify the expected response shape so repository results are consumed with compile-time type safety.
Demonstrates using the client to request a server error response and observe the resulting failure behavior.
Test helper that aborts an in-flight request and verifies that cancellation is surfaced promptly to the caller.

applicationFacts: The library exposes both a normal response-data interface and a raw response interface.
Requests support base URLs, query parameters, custom headers, JSON and form-style bodies, streams, timeouts, and caller-provided abort signals.
JSON-like request bodies are serialized automatically and receive default JSON content negotiation headers.
Response parsing is content-type aware and supports JSON, text, blob, array buffer, and stream representations.
Transport and HTTP failures are normalized into a FetchError with request, response, and parsed data context.
Retry behavior can be configured by count, delay, and eligible status codes; payload methods receive a more conservative default retry policy.
Request, transport-error, response, and response-error lifecycle hooks support instrumentation and custom middleware.
The Node.js entry point supports global fetch, a compatible fallback transport, and optional keep-alive behavior.
The package builds browser-oriented and Node.js-oriented entry points with generated type declarations.
Automated tests cover request handling, response parsing, retries, cancellation, error normalization, hooks, headers, query parameters, and payload formats.
unknowns: The repository's intended product positioning, supported runtime matrix, and release-management process are not established by the analyzed source.

No persistent data model, domain-specific entities, authentication workflow, or business lifecycle is evident; the repository appears to be a reusable HTTP client library rather than a business application.
